points.t: Painful, red, fluctuant nodule that **points** to a central pustule. Carbuncle: several heads.
*S. aureus* in the deep follicle → dermal abscess; recurrence suggests carriage, **PVL** or diabetes.
Moist heat; **incision and drainage** when fluctuant; flucloxacillin only with risk features.
PVL clusters, central facial boils, undiagnosed diabetes.

cause.lead: Your own staph, deep in a follicle.
points: Usually the patient’s own **S. aureus carriage** (nose, axillae, perineum).
Friction, shaving, sweat, minor trauma let it in.
Risks: **diabetes**, obesity, immunosuppression, close-contact sport, crowded living, household boils.

visuals.caption: Folliculitis (left) is superficial. A boil (centre) is a deep abscess around one follicle. A carbuncle (right) is several connected abscesses with multiple openings: it needs drainage.
visuals.alt: Three skin sections: folliculitis, furuncle and carbuncle

points: **Painful, red, hot nodule** that becomes fluctuant and points to a yellow-white head.
**Carbuncle**: larger indurated area, **multiple heads**; fever and malaise more likely.

items.name: Furuncle
items.t: Tender red nodule with a central yellow point.

items.name: Axillary abscess
items.t: Deep red fluctuant nodule; recurrent → think HS.

visuals.caption: Boil (left): one infected follicle with a deep abscess and a single head. Carbuncle (right): several neighbouring follicles joined by deep interconnected abscesses, with multiple openings.
visuals.alt: Skin sections comparing a boil and a carbuncle

points: If drained, recurrent, or PVL / MRSA suspected.

cards.name: Inflamed epidermoid cyst
cards.clue: Long-standing lump with a punctum that flares.

cards.name: Hidradenitis suppurativa
cards.clue: **Recurrent** nodules, sinus tracts, scars in folds.

cards.name: Folliculitis
cards.clue: Superficial small pustules; no deep abscess.

manage.lead: Drainage is the treatment; antibiotics are an add-on.

points: **Incision and drainage the same day**: primary care if skilled, otherwise surgical or urgent care.

rx.note: Only with fever, cellulitis, facial site, large / very painful lesion, diabetes or immunosuppression. Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy).

points: Screen for diabetes; discuss **PVL** and MRSA.
**Decolonisation** (nasal treatment + antiseptic body wash) via infection control or microbiology; household if advised.

limits.t: Don’t squeeze; lower threshold for antibiotics and review.
Own towel, hot-wash bedding, cover the lesion, wash hands.

visuals.caption: Small boils: moist heat (a warm compress) 3–4 times a day encourages spontaneous drainage. Don't squeeze, and use a separate towel.
visuals.alt: Warm damp flannel being applied next to a boil on the forearm

items.t: Boil on the **central face** or near the eye.
Spreading cellulitis, fever or systemically unwell; deep infection in diabetes or immunosuppression.
**PVL suspicion**: recurrent aggressive boils, household / team clusters, necrotising features → microbiology or public health.

pearls.t: ‘Recurrent boils’ in axillae or groin may be **hidradenitis suppurativa**.
Ask about household contacts and close-contact sport.

quiz.q: Treatment of a large fluctuant boil?
quiz.a: Incision and drainage, the same day.

quiz.q: When are antibiotics needed for a boil?
quiz.a: Fever, cellulitis, facial site, large or very painful lesion, diabetes or immunosuppression.
Flucloxacillin (clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic; erythromycin in pregnancy).

quiz.q: Recurrent painful boils in a rugby team?
quiz.a: Suspect PVL-S. aureus: swab, escalate to microbiology/public health, decolonisation.
